utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to everyone. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor against Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to say good morning to all those in the courtroom; the accused, the Prosecution, the Defence, and everybody else here. We're going to continue our work, and it is the cross-examination stage. But before we begin, I should like to turn to the Prosecution to tell them - we discussed this matter amongst the Judges - it would be advisable that if a witness comes in, that we could have a large map of the region put up, a really big map, so that we can see the different localities straight away. So would you do your best to find a large map and an easel or something of the kind that we can bring in and take out so that everybody can see where the places are and then the witness can take up a pointer and say, "I went to such-and-such a village," et cetera. That would be a practical way of going about things. As far as I'm concerned, I would like to ask a few questions of the witness before the cross-examination begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, could you tell me more specifically whether in the mission that you had with BritBat that on a medical level you also had the duty of bringing your aid and technical assistance to the local population. Was that within your remit as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our remit was very -- was primarily the medical care to UNPROFOR -- UNPROFOR troops and associated international agencies as laid down in -- in our mandate. Additional assistance that we could give to local populations with regard to medical care was only that of lifesaving assistance. And with regard to the distribution of aid and humanitarian-type assistance of that nature, anything that we did was cleared through our command structure. So for myself, that was through both the Cheshire's Battle Group and the National Support Element based in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Yesterday, you explained to us that as far as vehicles are concerned, well, that you went through a number of localities. When you were in these vehicles that you used, with an interpreter, was it to take aid and assistance to the population that was endangered, or was it simply to go around and for you to see the locality? I would like to hear from you the exact object of your travels in that locality, and was there a medical goal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- as I said yesterday, the main purpose for all of our visits as a battle group was as directed by OC B Company. If -- if they felt that it was appropriate or of assistance to them for us as medical call-signs to be on the ground as well, then that is of course what we did. That might be for various reasons. One was to provide integrated medical support to our own convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you're not answering my question exactly. You're telling me that the -- that you did what the commander of the company or battle group decided. Now, let's take a hypothetical, that the battle group commander told you to go to Dusa, for example, the village of Dusa, and you arrived in the village of Dusa. Now, when you got out of your vehicles, did you ask the first person you encountered whether they needed anything, or perhaps the other locals needed any medical assistance? Is that how you went about your mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in a village, I may or may not be -- in fact, I was very unlikely to be the convoy commander. I would most likely be an assistant within that convoy, although that didn't mean to say that I was necessarily not the most senior person on the ground from a rank structure. The modus operandus was such that we would arrive in the village. As I say, mostly the village, by the time we arrived, knew we were coming, presumable through messages passed on from checkpoints along the way, but our modus operandus was to meet with the village commander rather than just the first individual who we met. Having spent some time on the ground before the fighting started, it was usual but not inevitable that we would know who that individual was, and therefore if we met somebody different, we would ascertain what had happened to the person who we'd previously met, as to whether they'd moved on, were just away from the village for the day, whether they had killed or whatever had happened. So it was always the first person we'd aim to meet would be the village commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if the village commander happened to say to you, "I have in my village somebody who has been wounded or injured," would you have seen to that person straight away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not within our remit so to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't understand then. I asked you to tell me what your remit was, and you told me that my remit was to deal with UNPROFOR personnel and international organisations. I understand that. Then you added that you could also come to the aid and assistance of the local population. Now, I'm placing you in the following situation: I say you're in a village. The head of the village tells you there's somebody who has been wounded or injured, and you say, no, that's not with my remit to deal with that, to attend to that. So I'm trying to understand, to get a better understanding of why a doctor should find themselves in a vehicle belonging to BritBat in a village, and what would the doctor do in that vehicle in that village? That's what I'm trying to glean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our -- if I remember my wording reasonably accurately from my previous, it was to give lifesaving treatment. So if somebody required cardiopulmonary resuscitation, for example, we would do that, but to tend to somebody who had a broken leg, that would be outside of our remit. Why was I as a doctor on the ground? As well as being a doctor, I am a British army officer and therefore carry two kinds of role, job, whatever within my -- within my remit and so I'm a -- part of -- part of the battle group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, very well. You are doctor first and -- first and then a British army officer, or is it the other way around? Are you a British army officer first and a doctor second? What would you say that was the main function of these two? I can see that you're smiling, but give me a more precise answer, please. Would it be the doctor that stands above the British army officer or the other way round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those circumstances, allowing for the fact I was wearing British army -- British army uniform and wearing an UNPROFOR insignia, I saw myself very much as an officer first with additional skills as a medical officer. In my peacetime location, my day-to-day work for, like, for example, at the moment, I see myself as a doctor in -- first and an officer second. So the two are interchangeable, dependent upon the situation in which I find myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Thank you for giving me that explanation. And my last question is this: On the basis of what you've told us, it would appear that around the 13th of January, there was an offensive by the HVO. When the offensive started, were you in Gornji Vakuf when the HVO offensive was launched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Gornji Vakuf, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Now, when there's a military offensive, in principle there's the artillery, there's shooting, and so on. Now, in Gornji Vakuf did you hear cannons firing? Did you hear shooting noises or things like that? Was the offensive characterised by the usual sounds that accompany an offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, after that, your commander and you yourself, did you foresee that if there was artillery shooting, artillery fire, there could also be wounded, whether they be soldiers or civilians, and that in such a case you yourself could give urgent medical aid if the need arises, if there were no other doctors there? So would that be something that you would take into account at your level and at the level of your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My -- my remit is very much with regard to the treating of UNPROFOR personnel and -- and the agreed -- agreed international agencies. My remit was not to provide medical support to the local community, be that military or civilian, other than to provide acute lifesaving, for example, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, CPR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So -- but you seem to be repeating the same thing. I think that I understand what you're telling me, but you always seem to give the same answers. But fine. I have no further questions. What about my colleague? Perhaps the Judge -- no? I'm now going to give the floor to the Defence. I don't know who is going to start off. Counsel Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Carter. My name is Vesna Alaburic, I'm Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic, and I'm going to start off our conversation today with the questions that were asked by His Honour Judge Antonetti. Last night in the UN Resolutions about UNPROFOR, I tried to establish what the remit of UNPROFOR was and to what measure it coincides with your testimony yesterday about your activities in Gornji Vakuf. So may I ask you some very specific questions now. Would you agree with me when I say that the mandate or remit of the UNPROFOR was completely regulated by United Nations Resolutions? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me that in no Resolution of the United Nations is there mention of the fact that any military unit or any medical unit within a military unit would be authorised in any way whatsoever to give medical assistance to the local population, including even intervention in acute situations such as the ones you described? And I'm talking about UN Resolutions there.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't personally read the UN Resolution document, but that was my understanding of my roles and responsibilities and remit at the time, was -- as was I've -- as I've described. My understanding was that we would be allowed to give CPR, for example, at the side of a road traffic accident, for example, but nothing above and beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to make a comparison with a traffic accident. I was going to draw that parallel. When you leave this building, for instance, you come across a traffic accident that has occurred just outside the building and you see that somebody needs to be given medical assistance. Would it be your task as doctor to go up and help that person?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you -- if you felt that you could be of assistance, if the situation allowed you to do that, and there was no other medical assistance around, that is a decision that -- that you take yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you agree with me that, according to UN Resolutions, a military unit such as BritBat were not authorised to distribute humanitarian aid but, rather, were authorised to secure or provide escort to organisations which were authorised to distribute humanitarian aid, such as the UNHCR and the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, I haven't read the mandate, but that was certainly my -- my understanding. And if we wished to do anything outside of that, then we needed to clear that through our chain of command through to higher formations, and however far that went up is -- is beyond my scope.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Dr. Carter, whether in your opinion the commander of your company was authorised to issue you and other members of the company with tasks which were not in conformity with UN Resolutions which determined the mandate and remit of your unit.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order -- in order for the tasks to be given that were outside of the mandate to which you refer, I have every belief and opinion that the commander of the company would have sought authority from his chain of command and upwards as they deemed necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We'll get to that higher commander and whether he can issue orders that would be contrary to UN Resolutions about the mandate of individual military units. Would he?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your commander could have been ordered something by the commander up above. Now, let's get to the top-most level in the chain of command the top-most commander. Now my question is this: Would the main commander be able to give instructions to his subordinates which would be contrary to the UN Resolutions?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer for what my -- my superiors do or don't do or their thought processes that go with it. I work to the direction I'm given on the ground. I'm not sure I fully understand the purpose of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I must confess that I share the puzzlement of the witness, and I don't understand how you can ask the witness about her superiors' attitude towards their superiors. I don't know where you're going and what the link of these questions to our case are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you exactly where I'm going. We are trying to establish whether the witness was acting in accordance with the mandate established by the UN Resolution. When asked whether the instructions given to her were in accordance with the UN Resolution, she replied that she reacted according to the instructions of her commander and that she did not know whether this was actually in line with the UN Resolution or not, but in her view the most important fact was that she was acting in accordance with her commander's instructions. As in every army, and so I assume in the British army as well, the question arises as to the relation between a command and a rule on the basis of which, or an order on the basis of which it is issued. My further questions related to the difference and the discrepancy between the UN Resolution and the orders received by the witness, who toured villages in BritBat vehicles and carried out the activities she described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm -- with due respect, I still fail to see the link to our case here, which is not the case of proper or improper behaviour of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I do apologise, but I think it's my duty to give the reasons for my standpoint. I think it's very important to establish whether UNPROFOR or any UNPROFOR unit was carrying out its mission on the ground in accordance with the UN Resolution or whether they were overstepping their mandate. I feel that all local forces on the ground, including the HVO, felt that -- or, rather, that they believed that the UNPROFOR and all other such units were carrying out their mandate. If it transpired, however, that UNPROFOR vehicles were transporting items not in accordance with their mandate, the question arose as to whether they were overstepping their authority, and this gives rise to a number of questions I feel are relevant in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Your answer was really helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Carter, please tell us whether, to the best of your knowledge, it was usual on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when there was an offensive on a certain territory, UNPROFOR forces which had their headquarters on that territory would be temporarily dislocated to a safer area. For example, during the offensive or the combat activities in Mostar, the headquarters of a certain UNPROFOR unit might be temporarily relocated to another town for reasons of security.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my time in -- in this particular operational tour, I remained in the same location in Gornji Vakuf, less the detachment down to Tomislavgrad. We never moved our location, and there was never talk of us moving our location.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Carter, I wish to compliment you on your memory of the names of villages in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm sure that, as a native of Britain, these names sound very strange to you. I will therefore ask you about certain circumstances which will be of importance to us in determining the quality of your memory. You told us that the hostility between the Muslims and the Croats in Gornji Vakuf began around the 13th of January. Can you tell us how long that HVO offensive lasted, to the best of your memory?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- my memory is the fighting started before the 13th of January. 13th of January sticks in my mind as a date because that was the date of the death of Corporal Edwards, and that was the first time I personally had to deal with a combatant death, and that's therefore a date that sticks in my memory forever. And therefore, the majority of my -- of my date recollection is based around from that, so I can say that the starting -- the fighting started a number of days before that, and the issue of how long individual offensives lasted is quite a difficult question because there would often be brokered cease-fires that lasted short periods of time and cease-fires that lasted for several days or longer, so I feel that it's difficult to say exactly how long the first offensive last -- lasted. But certainly after the death of Corporal Edwards a cease-fire was brokered that afternoon, for example, which I do not recollect how long it lasted, but certainly within a short period of time the -- the fighting had resumed. So that's how the pattern of life became.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you used the word "offensive" in the plural, I wish to ask you what you understand by the term "offensive."

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'm using it in the plural, it -- it's as much -- it's as much to do with talking about each individual spell of -- spell of fighting rather than necessarily in the true military term -- in the true military understanding of the term, because clearly there will be breaks in fighting within a military offensive, but that's not the way in which I meant it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would I then be correct in concluding that in your view an offensive is in fact a military conflict?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you described two incidents to us which indicated that there were rising tensions between the Muslim and Croatian populations in Gornji Vakuf in late 1992 and early 1993. One of these incidents had to do with the flag in early January. You remember that. I will put a few questions to you in connection with this. Do you know what is referred to by the term "Ustasha"?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustasha was a flag -- a flag that was used by a --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I do apologise. I'm not asking you about the Ustasha flag but about who the Ustasha were.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustasha I understood to be a militant element of the HVO. A -- a military -- sorry, not the HVO -- a militant element. It had a militant meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, what did the Ustasha flag look like? What kind of flag was it that these militant elements used?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can -- I cannot recall the -- the -- the flag -- the flag itself. As I say, I was not on the ground at the time. I'm ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell us, did you make a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 7th and 8th of September, 2005, in connection with these events and your mandate?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made -- I don't remember the exact dates, but it was in September, 2005, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In that statement, do you remember mentioning the flag incident?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what you said then?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember talking about the -- the flag, the burning of the flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: With Their Honours' leave, I will put to you a part of your statement. In point 18 - in the B/C/S text that's page 7 - in connection with this incident, you said the following, and I quote from your statement: "I recall that a BH flag was raised either next to an HVO flag or in a predominantly Croat area. The Croat community were enraged by this act and pulled the flag down. At or around the same time a handicapped Muslim young man who I believe to have been wheelchair bound was in the vicinity of the flag pole." And so on. I will remind you of your testimony of yesterday referring to the same incident. It is recorded on page 47, lines 18 to 24, and I will read what you told us. I will read it out in English because the record is in English. [In English] "... I was not actually on the ground to witness it myself; and secondly, after 12, 13 years, my memory's not entirely accurate as to the exact details. What I do recall is that it was -- in my memory it was very much BiH, but I'm only aware -- aware of one flag-raising incident, so I would be -- I would believe that that is the incident to which I referred and that I was incorrect in the recollection of which side had raised the flag." [Interpretation] This is what you said after repeating what you said in your statement of 2005 and after the Prosecutor showed you an exhibit mentioning an Ustasha flag which you now tell us you did not know what it looked like. Can you explain how it came about that in the statement you describe the incident in one way and in your testimony of yesterday, and after the Ustasha flag was mentioned to you, which you don't know what the appearance of it is like, you changed your testimony. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I have changed my testimony. I -- I'm sorry, I don't -- I don't see that I have changed my testimony, so I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the statement of 2005 which I read out to you, and the same thing was stated by you yesterday, the BH flag was raised. However, after the Prosecutor intervened, you mentioned the raising of a so-called Ustasha flag, and that was why I'm asking you which flag was being raised and what caused the incident.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have always recollected the event as a -- as a BH flag. I have never said that it was an Ustasha. I have accepted that after 12, 13 years and not having been on the ground, that it may well have -- that -- you know, I was incorrect and -- you know, and that's how -- how I see it. So I don't believe that I have changed my statement, nor have I ever stated that it was an Ustasha. So I haven't changed my statement. I stand corrected but not changed my statement, and that's different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In that case, may I conclude that you abide by the description of this incident in your statement of 2005 and your original testimony of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my -- my memory -- my memory as it -- as it -- as it is was with the BH flag. I stand corrected that that may not have been the case and that over the period of time, you know, it -- it's -- you know. So I accept what I recollect, and I accept that --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now some brief clarifications of your testimony of yesterday before we move on. When you spoke about the distribution of aid in the villages - and this is found on page 54, line 19, of yesterday's transcript - you said, inter alia, the following: That you often crossed over from HVO territory into Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you explain to us what in your view is the relationship between HVO territory and the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect saying Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was talking about going from BiH Muslim-controlled territory to HVO Croat-controlled territory or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you mentioned the death of a British soldier on the 13th of January. Tell us, the British investigation which you say was instigated, did it yield any results?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's standard procedure whenever any soldier is badly injured or killed on a British operational tour that an investigation is opened, and depending on the findings of that initial investigation and subsequent advice through the Royal Military Police side of life and the army legal service, again I have no understanding of how they decide to proceed or not proceed in any individual case, nor do I -- and nor do I know how far they got with this investigation other than I know that they were -- they did open a case because they came to -- to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us whether to the best of your recollection in the course of the investigation into this event, was there any mention of the possibility that there had been sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "sniper fire" was and is used in two contexts. You can use the term "sniper fire" officially meaning a formally trained sniper with a sniper rifle and sniper bullets, or you could use the term more colloquially to talk about, you know, just people who are a good shot or whatever. And you can use the term just in general, in general terms, somebody sniping at somebody else, not meaning with weapons at all. So -- so with -- with regard to the possibility that there had been sniper fire, I'm sure amongst the troops on the ground and not on the ground it is -- it is quite possible that people did talk about sniper fire in -- meaning any of the aforementioned descriptions thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to your information, was sniper fire used by both the Muslim army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regards to the disposition of actual --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, it was not something that was of particular interest to me unless it was going to cause me threats, for example making my life difficult, but where sniper positions may or may not have been is of no consequence to me as -- in my role.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness document 4D 0037.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a request --

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I assume it will come up, and while we are waiting -- do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who issued this request? If we can scroll up so that we can see the signature. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can ask whether the witness saw the document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the HVO tried to establish the causes of the incident?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned in my statement yesterday, I understood that the HVO were in -- involved in an investigation themselves, yes, I was, as I stated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a request by my defendant, Milivoj Petkovic, addressed to Mr. Siljeg, who is a person known to you, in which he asks for information on the deployment of forces, both HVO and of the Muslim army, in order to establish how it came about that a British soldier was killed. Were you aware of a document such as this and a request such as this one coming from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I was not aware of -- of this request, nor have I seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a technical problem. I can no longer hear the interpretation. It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Carter, we will move on to another group of questions relating to cease-fires, and yesterday you told us that you had attended some of those meetings. Would you agree with me that you were aware of other attempts to reach a peaceful resolution of the conflict between the Muslims and Croats in Gornji Vakuf in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there were -- that -- that there was a lot of effort by -- along the way for establishment of and maintenance of cease-fires throughout -- throughout the period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will skip over the attempts made in 1992 in view of the fact that you remember the first conflict as having taken place in late December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I therefore wish to show the witness document 4D 00041.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by my defendant, the Chief of the Main Staff, Milivoj Petkovic. It's dated the 6th of January, 1993, in which, in order to fulfil the obligations that stem from the Geneva conference, he orders respect of the cease-fire and suspension of combat activities. And this order was issued in three operative zones with the headquarters in Tomislavgrad, Mostar, and Vitez. Were you aware of the efforts made by the HVO as early as the beginning of January to calm down all tensions and contribute to a peaceful resolution of the conflict between the two ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated previously, I was aware that there was a lot of effort along the way for the establishment and maintenance of cease-fires. Individual directions and individual authorities such as that - I haven't seen the document before - I -- I wouldn't have sight of in the role that I carried out, nor would I expect to have been -- been party to individual directives that were -- that were issued in line with this. I wouldn't have expected to know that -- that such a document existed or been expected to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, this document is dated 6 January, 1993, and the order is that by 10 October, 1992, certain records are to be forwarded. I must confess that this is a bit difficult to grasp. There must be something wrong. Is there an explanation? It's not a matter of translation, because the original document has the same dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My client will explain. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] There's a mistake there. It says October. It should be January. And the year is wrong too. Now, the second order that went out has the correct date. It's not October. It is obligations that stem from the Geneva conference, which began in January, 1993. So it's a mistake. It is not October. It is January, 1993, immediately upon conclusion of the Geneva conference in January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you to the Judge for clearing -- helping clear that up. There'll be other mistakes like that, but we'll take them as they crop up and explain them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the 13th of January. The date you mention is very important, for understandable reasons, because, unfortunately, your colleague fell casualty. The Chief of Staff, Milivoj Petkovic, issued another order, and may we have the document placed on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 4D 00045. That is the number of the document. If we might have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we go on to the next document, you're going to ask for the documents to be tendered into evidence when the time comes. This particular order that we were dealing with of the 6th of January, the witness said she hadn't seen it, but does she know that the request was made for a respect to be shown for the cease-fire? Does she know about that? Because that would allow you to tender the document into evidence. If not, we can't admit it. So I'm going to ask the witness. That will be quicker. You were shown a document, and you said that you had never seen it before. Now, my question to you is the following: Before the 13th of January, as you were a British army, as you told us a moment ago, first and then a doctor second, so as a British army officer, did you know, when you had meetings with other officers, that the HVO had issued orders according to which the cease-fire was to have been respected and maintained? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't recall particular reference to a particular document. As I say, my recollection is of at cease-fire meetings, if cease-fires were brokered and agreed, that -- and therefore by definition both sides had agreed to that, that then the message -- the message was to be passed down to troops on the ground that those cease-fires were to be adhered to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, in the same line, excuse me if I police again, as it were, I think that it is quite obvious that these internal HVO documents are unknown to the witness, and I find it very difficult to ask the witness to comment upon these documents. It seems to be a way of indirectly having your client in the witness stand by these written orders. I really wonder whether this is the correct method to introduce the former behaviour of your client before the Trial Chamber. Can you explain why you think that this is perfectly correct, because I'm sure that you think that, otherwise you wouldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for the question and giving me the opportunity of explaining. In view of the fact that the witness told us that she attended certain negotiations on the establishment of a cease-fire and a truce, and since this witness furthermore confirmed the contents or parts of the contents of certain military reports of the units -- unit to which she belonged, and since this witness considers herself to be a member of the British army and considers that part of her military remit and mission was that, I attempted -- I thought that it was a good idea to clarify the contribution made by the HVO to the peaceful settlement of conflicts and disputes. And in that context, I had -- had expected the witness to say that she didn't know the orders or some of the orders or HVO documents. I was prepared for that. But I thought that she could know something about the attempts made by the HVO regardless of the fact that she didn't know about those documents, and that would also be important from other sources, to learn about the attempts made by the various sides to solve the conflict peacefully. Apart from that, I consider that all these documents throw light on the context in which the events took place. So my questions were geared in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I apologise, but I'm going to ask a complementary question of the witness which goes along the lines of what my colleague has just said and you have just said. Madam, or Doctor, or Colonel, I don't know how to address you exactly. I'm going to call you "madam." Madam, you mentioned the 13th of January, 1993, and you said that there was a conflict that was ongoing at that time. You said that a moment ago. Now, your command, did it rally on that same day, the conflicting parties, that is to say the HVO and the representatives of BH, in order to arrive at a cease-fire? We have an order here. It's a strict order which says that the cease-fire must be respected and observed. There is a conflict going on. We don't know who is doing the shooting exactly, the firing exactly, but did your authority immediately ask the representatives of the HVO and the BH to meet in order to broker conditions for a cease-fire? So that is the question that goes along the lines of what we were able to read in the document. To the best of your recollections, of course. If you remember, fine; if you don't, fine again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The -- the two local commanders were invited to UNPROFOR base that afternoon in order to broker a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's important. Thank you. So on the 13th of January, 1993, in the afternoon the two local commanders went to the UNPROFOR base. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would also, if you allow, like to ask a question going a little step back to the order of the 7th January, I believe it was, where the Accused Petkovic ordered that the Geneva Conventions be respected. Did you note any difference in the behaviour of HVO troops after that date? Could you observe any effect of such an order even though you did not know the order itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I previously stated, from early January time until the 13th of January, I personally did not go on the ground, so I wasn't able to have any feelings from that point of view. With regard to sitting in -- in the base, it -- it was not evident, nor would I have expected it to be evident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse us, Ms. Alaburic. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do excuse you, and of course welcome interventions of the kind in the future. I think they're very useful to us and will help me in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Carter, when you say the local commanders who came to your base, who do you mean? Who were the local commanders?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "local commanders," that was the term that was used for who I perceived -- who -- who I understood to be the two -- the senior HVO representative and the senior BH military representative, both military representatives. My -- I do not recall their -- I do not recall their names, although they were people who at the time we met on several -- quite a lot -- quite a lot of -- quite a lot of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like you now, with respect to the document that's still on our screens, to take a look at point 3, if you will. So it is an order by Milivoj Petkovic, dated the 13th of January, and in point 3 of that order -- may we -- if we don't have point 3 -- yes, we have it now. So point 3 of this order states: "Prevent any attempts of lower commands to solve the problems by using force." In that connection, I would like to ask you the following: Do you have any knowledge whatsoever to the effect that local commanders would act on their own or that they would undertake action without the knowledge, let alone permission, from their commanders?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge either way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, your commanders, apart from having contacts with the local commanders, did they attempt to contact the higher commanders of the HVO and BH army in order to broker a cease-fire or peace in the area of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned yesterday, there were times when higher commanders clearly had been involved in brokering cease-fires or peace in the area of Gornji Vakuf. For example, the meetings to which Colonel Siljeg attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, the meetings that Colonel Siljeg attended, who was the BH army representative of his rank, his opposite number?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You don't recall. Thank you. Tell us, please, do you remember all the attempts made, or do you have any knowledge about all the items made on the part of the HVO up until the end of January - let's start with that, the end of January, 1993 - for arriving at a peaceful settlement, for issuing instructions to calm the situation, to contact the Muslims, to attempt to solve problems through negotiation, to avoid conflicts, to stop any military intervention, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be highly unlikely and unreasonable for me to know of all the attempts made, but I'm aware that attempts were -- were made, certainly those UNPROFOR was involved in. And as I previously stated, there were -- there were -- felt like regular meetings to meet and discuss implementation of cease-fires or to discuss cease-fires when they had broken down, to try and resurrect them. But I could not possibly know of all the attempts made.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did the conflicting parties, the Croatian side and the Muslim side, inform your command about events on the ground and their attempts to solve some of those problems themselves?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were good communications between ourselves and the two sides on the ground insofar as that with both military headquarters we had set up dedicated communication lines and radios, telephones, that kind of thing, so that they could keep us informed where they felt appropriate of what they wished to inform us of outside of pre-arranged or ad hoc meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Apart from that objective possibility for communication, did that communication actually exist in reality?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The conflicting parties, did they really inform your command about the situation on the ground, the incidents that broke out, the conflicts, and indeed their activities?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand -- my understanding is that as and when they felt appropriate, they -- they told us what they wished to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But do you have any knowledge about those reports or that information? Did it arrive on a daily basis? Would the Muslim side contact you more, or would the Croatian side contact you more, the HVO, or any more specific data about contacts made with your unit by the two conflicting parties?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I previously stated, there were pre-arranged meetings to which both sides would be invited. There would be shall we call them emergency meetings as -- as situations on the ground arose where either the meeting would be called by us and -- and I have recollection that there were times when either -- either side would say, "I think it would be helpful if we could meet on neutral territory to talk this through," and -- so I hope that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. That isn't an answer to my question. I didn't ask you about meetings. What I asked you was this: Telephone communication, for instance, or letters, correspondence, telefax, or any other type of communication on the basis of which one of the conflicting parties would inform your unit about events taking place on the ground and asked you to mediate, perhaps, or asked for your assistance or anything of that nature. It doesn't matter if you don't know about this, if you can just tell us.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that such -- such processes were in place, but it was not part of my day-to-day remit to be involved as such in the receiving or handling of such communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. But do you have any knowledge about those communications? Or I'm interested in knowing whether they went to you at all, did they address you at all; and, if so, how often? And did both the warring parties contact you equally frequently, or would you say that the Muslim side contacted you more frequently, for example, because it considered that you would help them precisely?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I was aware that communication -- lines of communication were open, lines of communications were used, but with regard to the balance between one side and the other using those lines and the frequency of the use of those lines of communications I'm afraid I'm not able to help you any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I won't belabour the point if you don't know. I wasn't ask you questions about a series of documents and HVO activities geared towards effecting a peaceful solution in Gornji Vakuf because you say you don't have knowledge of specific events, but I am just going to ask you about some of the documents we addressed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may we have Prosecution document P 01351 on the ELMO again, please, on our screens, on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Before we broach that subject, I'd like to go back to the previous document, because you asked the witness about it. You told me earlier on that the 3rd of -- on the 3rd -- 13th of January, in the afternoon, there was a meeting with local commanders with UNPROFOR. Were you present at that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't present at that meeting, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you weren't present, then there's no point in me going on with that question. Counsel Alaburic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were talking about P 01351, Prosecution document. And what I'm interested is on the last page of the BH text. In English it is on page 9, the beginning of page 9 of the English. So the beginning of page 9 is what we're looking at. The reference -- page number 9 begins -- there seems to be different -- a different numbering. It's not the same text as the one I have in front of me. I think we need page 8, the previous page, please. I do apologise, but it seems that the numbers are different. May we scroll down a bit? Yes. The part that begins: "A problem arose ..." I apologise. We seem to be encountering certain problems. It's on that page, but scroll down, please, further down. "A problem arose ..." Further down. There we have it. "A problem arose this evening."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So this is a report by Zeljko Siljeg, and you testified about that yesterday. And in this portion that I'm interested in now it says the following: "A problem arose this evening when an HVO checkpoint was put up in the village of Humac, and then the BH army immediately set up one near the mosque in the town." Now, I have a question in that regard. Do you have any knowledge whatsoever to the effect that the BH army would use its religious sites or the surrounding parts of the religious sites or the religious sites of the Muslim community, whether they would use it for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unaware as to whether the Muslim community were using religious sites for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness be shown Prosecution document -- a Prosecution document once again. I say "once again" because it was on yesterday. 01373. And I'd like to have the portion that relates to the village of Zdrimci. It's on the next page. Next page, please. About the joint commission, and then A is Zdrimci. That's right. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in this paragraph of your unit's report, it says the following, that in the village it was mostly the elderly people, women, and children who remained. And it also states that all of them wished to leave the village. Tell us, please, whether the conclusion and observation made in this report by your unit might not be correct. Do you have any knowledge that would point in that direction, that it might not be correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I cannot comment on the correctness or otherwise of a report that I was not involved in writing, other than to say that I would have no reason to believe that the reporting would be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have ten minutes before the break. So the next Defence counsel has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Coric has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor, in paragraph 72, said that Mr. Pusic is not indicted for the events in Vakuf, so I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's continue. Next. Mr. Karnavas. You've been very quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I -- thank you for noticing it. Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honour. We have no cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Counsel Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Carter.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: My name is Peter Murphy, and I represent Mr. Bruno Stojic. I just have a relatively few questions for you. You mentioned this morning that you had made a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in September, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And in connection with that statement, were you interviewed by representatives of the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interviewed by a lady called Susan Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Was that the first time that you'd been interviewed by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that would have been, then, approximately 13 years after the events about which you've been giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, your training is in the field of medicine.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You're a general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I understand from your evidence yesterday that you also have a training in gynaecology.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have training in gynaecology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Really. Then you --

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than as part of general medical training and that that goes with being a general practitioner, so yes, I have done a six-month obstetrics and gynaecology job, but that's only as part of general practice training, not as a gynaecologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Not as a speciality.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you had any formal training in forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of our standard entry officers course, we have a basic grounding in forensic medicine and then slightly more training with regard to collection of evidence as part of forensic -- collection of sampling, for example, as part of an ongoing police investigation, so working alongside the police to collect evidence in a way that they would require us to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, when you were assigned to -- when you went to Bosnia as a part of your assignment with UNPROFOR, however, you went as a medical officer.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You told us that your primary responsibility was providing medical care for UNPROFOR personnel.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you were not there as part of any kind of criminal investigation team, were you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I take it also that other than the basic training you've described, you have no particular expertise, then, in ascertaining the cause of damage to buildings.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Or of conducting interviews with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not interviewing witnesses, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You were not there in any kind of intelligence role, were you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And as I understand it, other than the -- the basic function of providing medical support for the UNPROFOR unit, you then took on an additional role in giving assistance to humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that was primarily because things were rather quiet on the medical front, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was more that the -- we were approached in order to do that because the fighting was intense, not that we are quiet. Our aim on military operations as medical personnel is to be quiet. We do not wish to be busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, that's what I meant. I think you said yesterday that you had the time because you were not unduly occupied, fortunately, with treating casualties among your own personnel.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's not why we took -- that's not why we took the task on. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But that task was one that you did for a relatively short period.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Between, I suppose, about February and April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. That sort of period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it was in connection with that work that you made visits to a number of villages in the Gornji Vakuf area.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated previously, our deployment on -- onto the ground was always under the direction of OC B Company, and if in the -- as a -- if as and when we were out we had opportunity to -- how should I put it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Perhaps my question wasn't clear. Let me -- let me try again. You describe visits that you made to -- as part of a convoy to different villages.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And as I understand it, on those occasions the convoy would be escorting some kind of humanitarian aid supply to the villages.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went on the ground it was not always to do -- to do that. It sometimes was, it sometimes wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. When you went there, in terms of communicating with the inhabitants of the villages, you were dependent on either having a local interpreter or finding somebody else who either spoke a little English or, in the case of the soldiers, perhaps spoke a little German.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The preferred and the norm was to use UNPROFOR interpreters. The second tranche would be to use the military interpreter, and the third tranche would be rarely used, would be that of predominantly the German speakers within our BritBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You told us that during the fighting itself you would remain on your base.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dependent upon the military requirements. There were times when military personnel -- medical personnel, rather, were required to deploy onto the ground in order to provide integrated medical support for the UNPROFOR troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But the information that you obtained and that you told us about yesterday was essentially what you were told by inhabitants of the villages.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And as a representative of an international force, you were probably aware of the possibility that you were getting one side of the story but not necessarily both sides of the story.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's 10.30. We're going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed with the cross-examination, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Dr. Carter, before the break I was asking you about your visits to different villages, and you explained that the preferred practice was to rely on UNPROFOR interpreters and that you were aware that some of the information that you got at least might be coming from one side of the rather than both sides of the story. Now, yesterday you described a visit to the village of Dusa. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you told us that you had been conducted around the village by one of the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you were rather glad about that, because you felt that was the safest way to proceed. You have to answer audibly.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that was because of the possibility there might be booby-traps or other dangers in the village.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I suppose during the period of the conflict that was always a possibility, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And so in effect, and I don't mean this disparagingly, but when you went to the villages, you would take the guided tour, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And this morning -- I just wanted to ask you about one point of your observation. This morning in answer to my colleague Ms. Alaburic, you gave an answer that you could not verify a report that you had not yourself written. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: With the registrar's assistance, could we please have on e-court Prosecution Exhibit 01351. I think we were looking at this earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: While I'm -- while that's being brought up, did you ever -- when you went around and surveyed the damage, did you ever take detailed notes about what you'd seen?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surveying damage was -- was -- was an aside to what we were doing other than to report on ballpark numbers and our perception of what we'd seen rather than doing a formal engineer's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I, as most military personnel, carry a small issued-style notebook into which you take notes at the time. In fact, they're identical to look at to police notebooks. So they're that size, carried in our -- carried in the pocket, and that gives you an idea of the amount of space that you have to write the details of -- of that that you wish to record, retain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, with the registrar's assistance, if we could go to page 3 of this document. Can you see the document now on the screen, Dr. Carter?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If we could go right to the bottom of the third page, please. Thank you. This is referring -- we rather scrolled past it, but referring to the village of Uzricje, and I want to ask, you see at the bottom there the statement, "A total of 24 houses destroyed (22 torched, 2 shelled)." Correct? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you remember yesterday Mr. Bos asked you a question as to whether that corresponded with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You remember you agreed that it did?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So can we take it from that, then, that you counted or had some note of a total of 24 houses being destroyed in that locality?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be in the -- I can't say I recollect exactly 24, but I do remember that when villages were all but destroyed there would usually be somewhere in the region of 90, 95 per cent of what we were shown that were -- that were destroyed. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I asked you a very specific question as to whether you agreed that a total of 24 houses had been destroyed in the village of Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be unable to say that it was 24 as opposed to 23 or 25 or any other such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But that's exactly what you did say in response to Mr. Bos yesterday, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I -- I can't remember exactly what I did say, but that that seemed a reasonable -- a reasonable number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: With the registrar's assistance could we now go to the bottom of page 5 of the same document, please. Do you see at the bottom of page 5 there, Dr. Cater, the statement, "A total of 18 houses and sheds were destroyed, of which 16 were torched and two houses were destroyed by shelling"?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Bos asking you if that also -- this is now referring to a different village, but he asked you if that also accorded with your recollection.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you said that it did.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And again, were you intending to give the Court the impression that you could confirm that exact quantity of damage?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was replying to -- that that was the order of the number of houses in these villages that we'd seen and that the idea of the majority of the damage being torching rather than shelling was in keeping with my recollection of the kind of damage that we found when we visited these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So then you were not intending to verify or confirm a report that you did not write. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Certainly. You were not, when you testified yesterday, trying to verify the contents of a report that you did not write yourself.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you did agree with Mr. Bos that the details in that report corresponded with your recollection.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With -- with the -- what would be the word? Would be in line with the -- 18 as opposed to 180, or 18 as opposed to 50. In other words, of the order of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move on then. With the registrar's help now, may we please go to another exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we go on to something else, I want to understand the distinction that you make between a house that is burning from a house that was gutted or destroyed. So how -- when you see a burning house, do you mean to say that the house was burnt because it -- fire was planted there, or do you mean to say that the house was destroyed from the shelling? Because in the report shown to you on page 3, there is a clear distinction between 22 houses that were burnt and two that were shelled. So you differentiate between torched, destroyed, burnt. How were you able to make those distinctions? A house could be burnt down because a shell fell on it, so it was torched. Of course, there were other causes that can destroy houses by means of fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When -- when we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I am speaking to the British officer in you now, not the doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When -- when we were looking at the houses, the -- those that had been damaged by shelling we took to be those where you could see the evidence of a large impact, with walls that had collapsed or roofs that had caved in as what appeared to be the primary cause, whereas those that we recorded as having been torched or burnt were those where it appeared to have little primary structural damage but where the -- where the fire appeared to have been the primary cause. It was based on the amount of -- you know, if there was evidence of a great big shell having come through the roof and that sort of -- and of course accepting that a great big shell having come through the roof may well have set fire to the building as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That was a very precise and clear answer, but in taking that further, you said that there could have been houses where the roof caved in and the house was on fire. So what was the cause of the fire? Was it caused by -- was it man-made, exterior, or accidental?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be impossible -- that would be impossible for me in my position to be able to comment upon that. I'm far from forensically trained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With the registrar's help, can we please look at Exhibit P 01068 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: While that's -- while that's going -- being found, Dr. Carter, I just want to return very briefly, although I know we discussed it already quite exhaustively, to the question of the incident where the flag was raised. You remember that, I'm sure. And you've been asked certain questions about that today also. You agreed today that you had testified and said in your statement to the Prosecutor, you described an incident involving a BiH flag; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that was to the best of your recollection what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that the incident had involved someone from the HVO tearing down the BiH flag; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But then yesterday, if you recall -- can you see the exhibit now on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If we can scroll down just a little bit, please. Thank you. Towards the bottom there, and it's rather hard to read now, I know - thank you - now at the top of your screen, Mr. Bos referred you to this document, an intelligence report which refers to an incident "at 1500 hours on Monday afternoon, the HVO raised an Ustasha flag in the town." You see that statement?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And in response to questioning today, you said that your understanding was that the Ustasha were an extreme wing of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I corrected myself to say that my understanding was that the Ustasha was -- was an extreme -- not necessarily of the HVO, just an extreme element of -- not necessarily the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So extreme element of what?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of -- of -- of an organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you don't know what organisation?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this context my recollection is that that's -- that that was with -- with regard to the HVO, but not -- not unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on. You recall Mr. Bos asking you about this statement and the intelligence report yesterday during your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And he asked you, did he not, whether, having seen this report, it might be that you were mistaken about the nature of that incident and this was really the flag incident that you were describing, the raising of the HVO flag instead?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you agreed with him that that might be the case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you said at that time also that you were only aware of one flag-raising incident.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only aware -- what I'm referring to is only one flag-raising incident that resulted in raising tensions at -- at and around that time. That was what I was aware of, just the one. That's not to say that more didn't happen, that's not to say that UNPROFOR didn't know about more. I'm saying what I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: This intelligence report would have been prepared from information received by UNPROFOR personnel, would it not?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my presumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I suppose what troubles me is that having been shown this, it appeared that you were ready then to agree with Mr. Bos yesterday that this was the incident in question, yet today in response to questioning from Ms. Alaburic, it appeared you were changing your mind again and saying, "Well, no, it was the BiH flag."

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I was sticking to what I had originally said in my statement, because my statement is that what I remember. I am more than happy to have my memory corrected, but I -- my understanding is that I -- you know, that I gave in my statement that which I believed to be correct. I stand -- if that is the same incident, which I have every reason to believe it is, I stand corrected on my memory, but as you have rightly pointed out, 13 years is a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I quite understand, Dr. Carter, and I sympathise. You're being asked to recall events a long time ago. My only concern is to clear that up, because it appeared that you were ready to agree with Mr. Bos's suggestion. But today you're telling us that the best of your recollection is the incident involved a BiH flag; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my perspective, I believe both of those statements to be correct insofar as my recollection is -- my recollection it was a BiH flag. I'm prepared to say that my recollection was probably incorrect and that I have every reason to believe that that is the same incident of flag raising insofar as it's mentioned in that report. The date -- the date/time group would be in line with my recollection. And as I said previously, I wasn't on the ground at the time so I didn't actually see the flag-raising myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you describe what the BH flag is like and what the HVO flag is like, to the best of your recollections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I'm suddenly surprised by myself because they were flags that we saw lots, and I have to say 13 years down the line it's not something that immediately springs to my mind to be able to describe in any great detail, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Just one or two -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the other hand, you could describe the Union Jack, could you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've lived with the Union Jack for 44 years, not just six months of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
