utterances.text: Just a couple of other things quite quickly, Dr. Carter. You described to us yesterday that you had been deployed as part of the medical unit a little ahead of the main battle group.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You arrived in October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You described an incident when you went to the building that you were going to use as your headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You said that in one particular part of that building you found what appeared to you be bloodstains and some cerebrospinal fluid.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In answer to a question from Judge Trechsel, you agreed that there had been no analysis of those substances.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were unable to undertake formal analysis. We carry standard British swabs for sampling to identify cerebrospinal fluid. The reason for that is that it contains protein and you can have swabs which will then undergo a colour change to say this is cerebrospinal fluid, important in cases where you have bleeding from an ear, for example. If you've got just blood, it won't change colour, but if you have the cerebrospinal fluid, it will. We did try swabbing the area but of course it was unlikely that we would be successful because it was clearly not fresh and therefore dried and therefore would not work. It's a test that works with liquid liquid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. My question is simply this: You made this discovery in October of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be on or around the 4th or 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again a date that is pertinent to the British insofar as the 5th of November is bonfire night, and I remember that we were already in the location on bonfire night and feeling that it would on this occasion not be appropriate for us to let off fireworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I know it was before the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay. We can agree, can we not, that that was before the outbreak of any ethnically based hostilities in the Gornji Vakuf area.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And the fact of the matter is that if crimes were committed in that building, you don't know who committed them.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You don't know who the victims were.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you don't know what any motivation for those crimes may have been.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Finally, on the occasions when you were -- went to villages as part of the humanitarian effort and accompanied a convoy with supplies, you told us that you had a system of delivering certain supplies on a 50/50 basis.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In other words, half of the supplies would be given to the -- the Croat side and half to the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: There was one occasion, was there not, when an HVO doctor told you that he had enough supplies and volunteered that you should give his share to the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And while understanding that you had certain difficulties at checkpoints from time to time, as a matter of basic principle you were theoretically able to deliver supplies both to the Croat side and the Muslim side; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically we were able to deliver supplies to both sides, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I mean, there were local difficulties, but the situation you encountered would certainly be consistent with somebody higher up having given instructions that those supplies were to be allowed through.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, in principle, you understood that supplies could be delivered both to the Croat side and the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And even though there may have been obstructions at a local checkpoint, that was the operating principle, that supplies should be allowed through to both sides.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Dr. Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may my client be given leave to put a few questions, after which my colleague, Ms. Pinter, may have a few brief questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Technical questions, go ahead, Mr. Praljak. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Lieutenant Colonel Carter. I have a number of questions for you, unless interrupted by Their Honours, to clarify the situation you have described. In 1992, when you arrived in Uskoplje or Gornji Vakuf, do you know where the joint lines facing the Serb side were located at the time?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I had and was given was predominantly related to what was going to be our area of responsibility, and as such was mostly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, madam. You have given long explanations when questioned by the Prosecutor. I am now asking you kindly to reply to my questions. If you know something, just say yes and explain, but if you don't know something, simply say, "No, I don't know," and this will enable me to put those questions, with Their Honours' leave, which I feel are relevant. It will give me enough time to do that. So my question is: Do you know where in October, 1992, the lines facing the Serbs were?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that the Serbs were a considerable distance from we -- from where I was based, possibly the far side of Bugojno, although I do not recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how much in percentages of those lines facing the Serbs were manned by the HVO and how much by Bosnia-Herzegovina forces?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. That towards the ends of 1992, after the fall of Jajce, when you were already in the area, aid to Jajce was stopped by Muslim forces at Ravni Rostov? Do you know about this or not?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. Jajce was not in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know that at that time trenches began to be dug around Uskoplje and Donji Vakuf by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that trenches were being dug within -- within our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: These trenches were very far removed from the forces facing the Serbs. The trenches were dug around the town where the transmitter was, the hills facing Prozor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not -- I do not know exactly where trenches were dug nor by which side trenches were dug. I was just aware that trenches were being dug because there was talk about the fact that some of the trenches were built to British army design.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. How many meetings were held in BritBat at which officers of BritBat attended in November and December, 1992, at which Colonel Siljeg and Colonel Andric participated on one single issue, to do something about the trench digging by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the town and around the town, which in military terms put the HVO in a position between two fires? How many such meetings were held in the British Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many such meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know in what manner the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was armed while you were there? Did the weapons arrive through HVO-controlled territory with the assistance of the HVO, or do you know of any other ways in which the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was armed?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know how the Bosnia -- the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that these fortification trenches made to British design put all of Central Bosnia into a position to cut all supply lines of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Are you aware of this or not?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know -- as I said earlier, I was -- it was only rumour that they were built to British design. I don't know for certain if they were or they weren't, and I wouldn't know what British design looked like anyway, and I was not aware of their intention or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So you toured villages around Uskoplje. Can you tell me whether you personally saw a single house being torched?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in a position to arrive in a village as a -- as a house was being torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So you did not. You did not personally see a single house being torched. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw the results thereof and still smouldering houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see a house being shelled, you personally?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in the NATO standard and in the Warsaw Pact standard there is incendiary ammunition which makes it very easy to set fire to buildings by shooting onto the roofs of the buildings? Do you have this information, as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know after the break-up of the Warsaw Pact, it was relatively easy to buy such ammunitions from the depots in Eastern Germany?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the witness has just said that she has no idea about such ammunition. I think there is no purpose in asking more questions on this. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know that there is incendiary ammunition both in the NATO standards and in the Warsaw Pact standards?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that such ammunition exists. Beyond knowing it exists, how it works, how you buy it, anything else, I know nothing about it. I -- I know it exists, but beyond that, I know absolutely nothing about incendiary ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, I'm not accusing you of ignorance. It's not your fault if you don't know something. Just simply say, "I don't know." When you were inside a building -- or, rather, in the small outbuilding where you saw the traces of blood and fluid, you said that a man named Avdo had been assigned to you.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- my recollection of his name is Avdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know that Avdo is a Muslim name, an exclusively Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If you established that there was no conflict at the time between the Croats and the Muslims and that the situation was peaceful, would a Muslim who evidently knew a lot about it conceal any possible crimes committed by the HVO, or was he perhaps the one who committed crimes against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no reason to -- to be in a position to be able to decide either way whether he was concealing crimes on either side. There was not -- that was not -- that was not the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I understand, but a Muslim was there, and I'm pointing to the logical absurdity of the situation, either of him concealing HVO crimes against Muslims or him together with other Muslims committing crimes against Croats, in which case he would have concealed the traces. Evidently, if one thinks logically, there may have been certain groups active in the area who did something, but this does not -- actually was not done by either of the two sides we're talking about. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's entirely possible, and no way along the line has -- I hope I haven't suggested that we were accusing anybody of any crimes. We were just making observations of what -- of what we saw, and my concern at the time was that these buildings would be fit and safe for occupation by BritBat forces and, therefore, we didn't want to put them at risk of touching dried blood, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were there, did you ever hear of the name Paraga?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recognise the name Paraga.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In that case, you cannot be aware of fact that he was the commander of a renegade group of HOS men which also killed two Italian humanitarian aid workers. Do you ever hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't recall that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in the village of Dusa --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, why are you asking these questions? What is the reason? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Relevance is what we're looking for. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the simple reason that without having the overall situation and complete knowledge about an area, such as Uskoplje and Gornji Vakuf, it is very difficult through partial information to arrive at the truth. That is why I am trying, by putting questions which I feel the lieutenant colonel is a relevant witness to answer, to find out about the informal renegade groups who were present in the area, about the possible ways in which buildings were set on fire, about the possibilities of identifying the perpetrators, the ability of commanders to control such a situation, about the possibilities of situations such as that described by the lady, a rape in a village without electricity, a remote village where four men arrive at night, enter a room and are recognised as being HVO soldiers in the dark, without any electric light, about a cellar which is dark. I want to know how big that cellar is, whether the lady had to kneel to get in, how it was possible to see blood there. So I want to know about all this. The lady talked about sociological matters, about the relative prosperity of Croats and Muslims. She spoke about who was helping whom from Germany and abroad. The lady is a major of the British army, but she doesn't know about the UN mandate, which was very strictly defined and related to humanitarian convoys, about the use of armed rights to the right and left of the road along which convoys are passing. And I want to ask, because the HVO, in the conflicts in Gornji Vakuf, had over 50 killed and more than 200 casualties in those conflicts, I want to know where those people were treated, where wounded members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were treated, why the conflict in Gornji Vakuf did not spread to Bugojno, who and how succeeded in keeping the peace there. All these are questions which need to be answered here. To what extent the lady spoke about the moving in of refugees after the fall of Jajce, to what extent the new refugees changed the make-up of the population, thus intensifying and speeding up the spiral of evil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We've understood. This could go on for hours, but take the essential, the main questions quickly. I'm not saying that the other questions are not relevant, but, unfortunately, we have time constraints. So focus on your most important questions and go through them as quickly as possible. But you will, of course, have an opportunity later on to broach these questions again. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Madam, when you were in Dusa and when you saw that cellar, how high and how wide was the window in that cellar, and how far above ground was it?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building had no windows, but it had the hole for where the window would be. My recollection is that the window was probably the size of one -- one of these desks, platforms, whatever you want to call these structures in front of us here. And it was the middle of the -- it was the middle of the day, so -- so it wasn't in the dark. And to look down was very little distance, as I said, because of the lie of the land, although it was -- the basement on one side, of course, it doesn't always become balanced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If the witness is referring to the desk, maybe she can give an approximate -- just in metres or feet, but -- for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess that's - I don't know - a metre by two and a half, something like that. Is that right? A metre -- a metre is three foot, yeah. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You stated here that there were many mixed marriages in Uskoplje. On the basis of what analysis did you conclude this? Did you carry out an analysis? How did you arrive at this information, and what does a lot mean in terms of percentages?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was information that we gathered in -- in those early -- in those early weeks when we were there from all sides, very much that war was -- was not what they wanted because they had this inter-ethnic -- inter-ethnic community in Gornji Vakuf. And so it came from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Madam, please. Let's be precise. From all sides. What sides are you referring to? Did you go to the municipality and look in the marriage registry books for the previous few years?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the -- one of the discussions that we did have, in fact, was with one of the municipality officers, who confirmed that there were a significant number of inter-ethnic marriages in -- or inter-ethnic families in -- in the Gornji Vakuf area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you carry out any kind of precise analysis such as you have to carry out when treating your patients?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the tie-in between analysis of the percentage of mixed marriages and me treating casualties or patients. I'm sorry, I don't understand how I would compare and contrast the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Very simply. Sociology, anthropology, ethnology, areas in which you have put forward a large number of conclusions here is science. It has its -- it's a discipline with its own methods and procedures. So I am asking you was it on the basis of precise data that you arrived at the fact that in Gornji Vakuf in such-and-such a year there was a certain percentage of mixed marriages? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the -- based on what you've said there, the strongest evidence, if you wish to call it that, would come from our discussions with one of the gentlemen from the municipality who gave us that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. You said that the Croats were more prosperous than the Muslims. You based your conclusion on television sets, microwave ovens, audio equipment. What was the representative sample on the basis of which you reached your conclusion? Do you know what a representative sample is?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know what a representative sample is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: How large was your representative sample, and what kind of research did you engage in in order to reach this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When -- when reaching that -- when -- when making that comment earlier, it was based on observation rather than true scientific evidence based. It would have been inappropriate for us to work -- spend time working out the socio-demographic discrepancies or variations between communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were in the village -- in a village after 20 minutes driving to the right from Bugojno, and there a female person told you that at night three or four men had entered her room, that they put their hands over her mouth, and that they raped her. These villages are 20 kilometres from Gornji Vakuf and are predominantly Muslim. As a doctor, did you establish in any manner whether there was a factual basis to believe the story? Because there was no electricity, it was night-time. Did you have any doubts, and did you carry out any kind of scientific or medical investigation to establish the truth of the story?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The story was given to us -- or was given to me based upon the lady volunteering all the information on -- as was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You have already told us what she told you. But you are trained in gynaecology. Did you check the story in any way? We've already heard what you said about this.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have -- it would have been inappropriate for me to have examined the lady to -- to corroborate or dispute her accusations. We just listened and passed the information to the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, throughout that time, with 50 dead on the HVO side and 230 wounded and most probably a comparable number on the BH army, you as a doctor, did you ever give medical assistance to anyone and, if so, to whom and when?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gave medical assistance to our own. We escorted the -- the BiH lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We've already heard that, madam. I asked you a simple question. Did you give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the witness was exactly answering your question. You were asking did you ever give medical assistance? You did not say to this or to that. It was an open question, and you interrupted her where she was exactly answering that question. She said, yes, I gave to this, and she has not finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had the same objection. I think the witness should be given a chance to actually finish her answer, because Mr. Praljak is constantly interrupting her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. Complete the answer to the question that was asked of you, and that was whether you yourself gave medical assistance to HVO soldiers who were wounded, and if -- possibly certain of them had been killed. And whether you did that also for the BH soldiers. So that's the question you were asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On no occasion did I treat HVO or BiH soldiers. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't take up more time. I just have one more question, and it is this: Was it part of your job as a doctor and also professionally as an officer to be unbiased and not to reduce the problem to the level of your own lack of knowledge? Or let me put it this way: Is it possible to explain a physical theory, Einstein's theory, with four arithmetical methods; addition, subtraction, multiplication, division? Is that possible? Can one do that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- my job as a doctor and as an officer is always to remain unbiased and to record and report that that I see with the knowledge that I have and to leave -- and when required, to leave others with broader knowledge and greater understanding to interpret that information which I give them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you didn't sociologically, politicogically and anthropologically study that.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean did I do a sociological, political and anthropological study of the Gornji Vakuf area, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Pinter or Mr. Kovacic, if you have any additional questions to raise, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. We have no further questions, and Mr. Praljak's Defence rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to ask the Prosecution whether they have any additional questions, but before I do that, I myself have a question to ask you, madam. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At Gornji Vakuf, the British Battalion was located at Gornji Vakuf. At what particular locality there?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located in a light sort of industrial-type factory on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a factory. Very well. Thank you. In an industrial zone; is that right? Does the Prosecution have any additional questions? Of course, questions arrived from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Prosecution doesn't have any further questions except that we would like to tender our exhibits. I don't know if this is the time to do that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see to that later on. Madam, you have completed your testimony here. Thank you for coming, having been asked to do so by the Prosecution, and contributed to justice. On behalf of the Judges present, and those absent as well, I would like to extend our gratitude and wish you all the best when you return to your country. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn to the Prosecution to hear the exhibit numbers, and then I'll ask the Defence the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has seven exhibits to tender, and I'll read out the numbers: 01068, 01113, 01308, 01351, 01373, 01386, and 01600.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So those are the documents that you would like -- that were presented to the witness. Mr. Registrar, do your duty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] The following seven exhibits are therefore tendered and admitted: 01068, 01113, 01308, 01351, 01373, 01386, and 01600. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now let me turn to the Defence with respect to the exhibits shown to the witness that the witness did not know about but that according to their contents could correspond to what she did know. Do you have the numbers for those?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to the criteria used by the Prosecution in tendering his exhibits, and these documents were ones that the witness did not know about nor could she confirm the contents of the entire document, I would like to put forward three exhibits that we showed the witness today. They are under the following numbers: 4D 00037, 4D 00041, and 4D 00045.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That makes it three documents: 4D 37, 4D 41, and 4D 45. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Those three exhibits are therefore tendered and admitted under the following numbers: 4D 00037, 4D 00041, and 4D 00045. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We shall proceed with the next witness, and we shall discuss protective measures. After we have discussed that, we need 30 minutes to change the tapes, so we will finish after that and reconvene in an hour and a half, after the lunch break. I can see that Mr. Karnavas wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I might make just one brief -- actually, two, two brief observations that might assist us in trying to save time in this courtroom in light of the limited time that we have to try this case. One example was this whole incident with the dry blood and the cerebral fluid. It wasn't until the cross-examination with my colleague Mr. -- Professor Peter Murphy and then again by the general that it was brought out and flushed out. Clearly the impression that the Prosecution wanted to leave yesterday that this blood or cerebral fluid or the incident that occurred in that location was the result of Croat or HVO activity. When we look at the time and the place and the events, it's clear that's not anywhere near. The dates are off, there is no real evidence, and the witness basically even today admitted that she didn't do the basic test because she could not. This is one area, for instance, that if the Defence did not challenge, it might lead the Trial Chamber to a wrong conclusion. I would suspect that when proofing a witness, the Prosecution knows that perhaps that's an incident has little or perhaps absolutely no value at all to this case, and in doing so they may be leading the Trial Chamber in the wrong direction, hence the difference between an adversarial system and a continental system. And since we're going more into a continental system, I would suggest that perhaps the Prosecution try to do its very best to pose questions that are strictly limited as opposed to perhaps introducing evidence that, if it go unchallenged, might lead the Trial Chamber in reaching a wrong conclusion. In a continental system, as you well know, the Prosecution has an obligation to bring up both inculpatory and exculpatory but also is there as an officer of the Court as he would be also in the Anglo-Saxon system. But there we have an adversarial process, here we should be closer to the continental in that respect, so I think we can eliminate time-consuming areas of confrontation if we just stick to relevant matters. Another -- my other observation goes to the questioning by General Praljak with respect to whether the doctor conducted any examinations with respect to the -- to the rape incident. I saw a reaction from the Bench. I thought I might want to comment on it. Had it -- had it been the victim herself here, I would say that we need to be very, very careful and gentle and perhaps even get some guidelines from the Court as to how far and to what extent we can ask questions. But I think if there's a witness here and the impression that the Prosecution wants to put on is that somebody was raped and was raped by Croatian HVO soldiers and therefore somebody among the crew over here is guilty, perhaps one or all of them, then I think it's only reasonable for the Defence to ask the medical doctor if indeed she conducted a relevant test. The answer was no. Mr. Praljak went on. I think it's appropriate to point out, because, after all, the Prosecution has to prove beyond a reasonable doubt. I suspect if they're going to insist that this rape indeed occurred by HVO soldiers, then of course they would need to bring in more evidence. But I think in that particular area it's perfectly appropriate for the Defence to go in, and again maybe these are the sort of things that at some point we may need some guidelines from the Trial Bench as to how far we can go in. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. I share some of your preoccupations when the examination-in-chief was conducted. It is true that a civil law Judge would have immediately asked the witness at what date she was in the locality in order to check and see whether what she's saying is included into the scope of the indictment, and then the witnesses would be defined that way, because it wasn't a rape -- if it was rape that occurred six months or one year before or outside the date of the indictment, then that would be another matter. So to avoid this kind of inconvenience, it would be a good idea that when a question is asked that seems to you be important, that the question should be situated in time and space, time especially, to see whether it comes within the frameworks of the indictment and what particular time, because to ask a question in January can be interesting -- relating to January, but much less so if the indictment refers to July. So try and be as precise as possible. Very often I myself have the urge to intervene because I find that there's an element lacking, but I place my trust in you, in the two -- and the two examples that you quoted highlight the difficulties that we encounter. But rest assured that we're not a jury. We are professional Judges, and we know full well how to attribute weight to what has been said in the courtroom, and it is only when we have all the elements before us that we make our final conclusions, because as you know, we cannot declare ourselves -- we have to declare ourselves beyond reasonable doubt. So rest assured -- both parties can rest assured that that is our concept of the matter. So any testimony that is imprecise will be viewed as being imprecise unless there is particular reference to dates, places, and so on which will give greater weight to the substance. It's 12.00. I suggest we have the blinds drawn and introduce the witness and hear what the -- what the witness has to say on the protective measures, after which we shall be taking a break and reconvening in an hour and a half. I'm saying this for the public gallery. And having said that, we're going to have a -- because of procedure, we're going to have to lower the blinds first. Do we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This would be an empty moment, as it were. I would like to comment on this issue on the rape and the question. I think, if I'm not wrong, the rape is not even in the indictment, so it is not really one of the facts to be proved. And second, I think with all the difficulty of our tasks, being involved in humanitarian law and human rights, we should not behave and expect behaviour which -- which is close to the inhuman. I imagine this situation. With my fantasy I go there. I see this woman who is probably crying, and then I imagine the doctor say, Oh, you were raped, will you come to the next room and show me. I think this is a behaviour that would be completely unacceptable on a human basis, and that is -- that is the reason why I reacted a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I share -- I share that level of humanity with you, Your Honour. However, if we're going to convict somebody based on that, we have to -- so as a lawyer, a Defence lawyer, I have to react, and at least I have to put -- chime in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, I would now like to ask you to stand and to tell me your name, surname, and date of birth before you take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, ladies and gentlemen, my name is Omer Hujdur. I was born on the 19th of April, 1952.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you tell me, please, what your present function or profession is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time I am deputy in the House of Representatives of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sir, have you already testified before an International Tribunal or national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992, 1993, or 1994, or is this the first time that you're testifying in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you now go ahead and read the solemn declaration handed to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm going to give you some information about the proceedings, because it is procedure that you are not accustomed to. In the first stage, you're going to be answering questions put to you by the representatives of Madam Carla Del Ponte, who is the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, and her representatives are sitting to your right, and I'm sure you've met them before during the proofing sessions. Once the representatives of the Prosecutor have completed their examination-in-chief, the Defence counsel sitting to your left will also have the right to ask you questions, which we call in common law procedure the cross-examination stage. And you will be able to see straight away that the way in which those questions are asked are different to the way in which the questions were asked you by the Prosecution, because during the cross-examination, we start out from a hypothesis and then you are asked to give a yes or no answer unless you need to go into detail. The Judges sitting in front of you - usually there are four Judges but today only two Judges are sitting because other Judges are otherwise engaged professionally - can step in to ask you questions at any time. As a general rule, we ask questions when we feel that something needs to be clarified with respect to the questions asked and your answers, and we feel that it is in the best interests of justice for us to ask you these questions. If in the course of being questioned by one or other party you experience any difficulties, please do not hesitate to let us know. And if you feel in particular that an answer that you have given necessitates you to go into private session, we will allow you to do so. Let me remind you that you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, and you know as a parliamentarian yourself that any mendacity, of course, entails repercussions, and I don't have to insist upon that any longer. So in general terms, that is a rundown of the way in which the proceedings are conducted. We normally work for one and a half hours, after which we take a 20-minute break, and that is for technical reasons, and then we reconvene after the 20-minute break. So we shall be working for an hour and a half, a 20-minute break, and then another hour and a half. Let me tell you that today we finish business by 5.00 p.m. If we have not completed the examination, then unfortunately, you will have to come back tomorrow morning. I mean unfortunately for you. But I hope we'll complete everything today. Without further ado, I'm going to ask a representative of the Prosecution to start the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour. Mr. President, just before commencing, if I may indicate the paragraphs in the indictment that the testimony of this witness are relevant to, are paragraphs 7, 17.3(a), 17.3(c), 33, 37, 43, 45, 46, 47, 48, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, and 59. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hujdur. Now, Mr. Hujdur, could you tell the Court, are you married and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes, I do have children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I grew up in Prozor, in the Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You went to school in Prozor as well?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes. After primary school, I completed the mechanical engineering school and then went on to study mechanical engineering at the university in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After completing your studies, did you return to Prozor?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I started my working life in a traffic company, communications company. Otherwise, I worked on the hydroelectric power plants at -- on the river Neretva and in the UNIS factory for a time as manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The hydroelectric plant, power plant, and the UNIS factory, are they in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes. The hydroelectric power plant is in the Prozor municipality. The lake is in part of the Prozor municipality, whereas the actual plant is some 15 kilometres away. And the UNIS factory is in the town of Prozor proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When did you enter politics in Prozor for the first time?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Well, professionally speaking, since the beginning of March and April, 1992. In more amateur terms I delved in politics a little earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From when? Referring to the more amateur politics, from when?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: In 1986 to 1990. I was representative of the Prozor municipality and Jablanica in the Republican Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the representative for the economy. It was called the Associated Labour Chamber in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But as I say, it wasn't a professional post. It was an amateur one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: For which party -- or to which party did you belong at that stage?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: At the time, I was -- it's the SDP now, but at the time it was the League of Communists, up until 1990 and somewhat later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You say that you remained in this party until 1990, or at least you performed functions in the party until 1990. What caused you to leave the party?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I left the party during 1991, among other things because of the very mild reactions of the party to the events that were taking place primarily in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: We will get to that in a short while. Can we have a -- can you give us a brief description of Prozor. The municipality of Prozor, how large is it?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The Prozor municipality is 400-odd square kilometres, the surface area. It's a medium-sized municipality when speaking of its surface area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Are you able to give an idea of the demographic composition of Prozor in the light of the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes. According to that census, the Prozor municipality had 19.702 inhabitants, of which 62 per cent were Croats, 37 per cent were Bosniaks, and 1 per cent were Serbs and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So the Croats were in majority in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What about the town of Prozor? What was the composition or ethnic composition of the town of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The town of Prozor at that time had 3.565 inhabitants, and we can say that approximately two-thirds were Bosniaks and the rest were Croats and Serbs and those who declared themselves as others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The two main groups, the Croats and the Bosniaks, did they live in separate areas in the town of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: We can't put it that way, no, although there were parts of town which were predominantly inhabited by the Bosniaks, but viewed as a whole, it was a mixed population structure. Now, in the part of down that was exclusively populated by Bosniaks, there was the Varos area and what is referred to as Carsija, or the centre of town, the lower part of the town of Prozor referred to as Carsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: There is a part in the town called Pogradje. What about that area?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes. That's a part of town which is on a hill, at an elevation above the town of Prozor, on the road towards Gornji Vakuf or, rather, in the eastern part of town, which was mostly inhabited by the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to 1991, what was the -- how would you describe the relationship between the ethnic groupings in Prozor, in the municipality and in the town?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The ethnic relationship between the ethnic communities or ethnic groupings, as you said, were traditionally good over a long period of time, right up until the end of 1990, in fact, until the end of the -- or, rather, the beginning of the multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you give the Court an indication from purely a common-sense point of view, as somebody who grew up in Prozor and lived in Prozor, about the geographic importance of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Prozor is a municipality, and the municipality headquarters, in fact, is to be found along the communication lines, the nearest communication line between the Adriatic Sea and Zagreb, or Dubrovnik and Zagreb. And it was very well connected, with the south towards Mostar and Metkovic and Dubrovnik and the Adriatic coast, and to the north Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Jajce towards Zagreb, and further on towards other destinations in Europe and the world. So that then is how it lies as concerns north/south, on the north/south line. Now, with respect to east/west communications, next to Prozor municipality is what used to be Duvno municipality, today it is Tomislavgrad, and Kupres. Prozor is connected to those places with a regional macadam road. And to the east it was linked to Konjic, also with a regional road but once again a macadamised road surface. We can say that communications, east/west communications were pretty poor, if you look at the quality of the roads, that is. Not very good roads along that line of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can turn to the elections -- I beg your pardon. If we can turn to the elections of 1990. The government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina called an election in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The elections were held on the 17th of November, 1990, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you participate in those elections for any party?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I did go to the elections. I did participate, but I wasn't on the list of any of the parties, because my mandate still lasted until the end of that year in the Republican Assembly or, rather, the party I was in. So I had no desire while being -- while working in one term of office or mandate to change my clothes, if I can put it that way, and go and take up a position for someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was the result of this election in Prozor municipality?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The results of the election was that the election was won by the HDZ and the SDA. They were the victorious parties of the Croatian and Bosniak people. And a small percentage of votes went to the SDP party, which was still a multi-ethnic party in composition. However, it wasn't the strongest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Which party obtained the majority or had the most votes?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The HDZ absolutely secured the majority vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The HDZ and the SDA parties, do you know whether they tried to come to some kind of power-sharing agreement subsequent to the election?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I really can't say that they went into a coalition or power-sharing agreement or an agreement of any kind. They did talk and discuss matters, but from the beginning there were things that they did not agree upon and problems cropped up. Now, if I'm allowed to talk about those problems now or perhaps in -- as you go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: We can get to these problems at a later stage. Could we first look at the structure of the municipal government in Prozor. What did the -- or how was the top structure of the municipal association composed?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The usual structure, just as in any other municipality, was that the Municipal Assembly acted as a municipal parliament or the legislative organ, and the president of the Assembly, also the President of the Executive Board or Prime Minister of the government of the municipality, if you want to put it that way, and the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, these were key positions, as well as the municipal departments for the economy, for town planning, for finance, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was there a mayor for the town as well -- or before getting to the mayor -- sorry, I withdraw that question. Just to make it clear, at the top we have the Municipal Assembly. Who does the Municipal Assembly -- or how is it composed? Who does it comprise?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: It was composed of delegates - I think that was their title at the time - of the Assembly. These were representatives of the ruling parties at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly, was he elected or appointed by these delegates? By the representatives of these.

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I think that he was elected. Whether it was the delegates who appointed him, well, I can't exclude the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In any event, who became the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Mr. Mijo Jozic, who was, of course, the representative of the HDZ, became the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The secretary that you referred to, who was the secretary, or who became the secretary?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Also a representative of the HDZ. Certain faults were linked to his name. It turned out he did not meet the requirements, because he had not graduated from university, nor did he have work experience. However, when objections were raised, the answer given was that one had to build up a modern administration comprising young people and that one day he would in fact acquire the necessary conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly and the secretary, could they be described as the executive within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Council represented the executive branch of government, and he was also a representative of the HDZ. Only his deputy, at a lot of insistence, was appointed but his powers were negligibly small. They were marginal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who was the president of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: A representative of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know who he was or who was appointed to the position?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: At the time, it was Nikola Ivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: As you say "at the time," was Nikola Ivic later replaced?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Later on another man would be appointed, but a lot later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Within this top structure of the -- sorry, before going there, you mentioned that beneath this structure that you've just described there were also departments. Could you perhaps give an idea of what these departments were and what their functions were. In general terms.

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The department for town planning, the department for inspections, the tax administration department. That was given to a representative of the SDA. But at that time, to hold that post, as at any time, well, it's highly responsible, a highly responsible job to work in the tax administration. It's a difficult job. Then there was the inspections department. An SDA representative was there as well. And as I said, where Bosniak representatives were appointed, those were the less important posts, and posts which were difficult in terms of the job that had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were there any posts which had specifically been promised to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes. Just a little while ago, I mentioned the problems that arose at the very outset of establishing the government after the elections. One the important posts which had been promised to the Bosniaks was the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff for Prozor municipality. Throughout this time, it was a bone of contention. Well, I won't put it quite like that, but one might say that because a promise had been made but never followed through by representatives of the HDZ, and this remained opened -- open throughout this period. Nobody was actually ever appointed to that post, and this gave people a bad feeling with regard to representation, equality, confidence, safety and security, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you left the SDA party in 1991. Did you join any other political party?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: There might be a typing error here. I left the previous party in the second half of 1991, and for six months I was not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apologies. When did you again join a political party?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: In essence, at the invitation of the Crisis Staff, I joined the talks aimed at calming down tensions and alleviating the very bad atmosphere prevailing in Prozor in late March and early April, and they didn't even ask me whether I was an SDA member or not. However, at that time it was only possible to be active within the scope of the existing options, and at the request of representatives of the then SDA, and of course other people, I formally became a member of the party on the 24th of June at the Assembly of the party -- the party convention, rather, in June. And from March to April one might also consider me to have been a member of the party, but in formal terms I became a member at the party convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the period that you're referring to, March to April, is that 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one step backwards for a moment. During 1991, the HDZ party in Prozor, did they hold any rallies or gatherings?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I remember a large rally held on the shores of the Ramsko lake. It might have been an anniversary of the HDZ party. And at that gathering many people were present. Their passage through the town was unusual and disturbing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did this have any -- was there any reaction to the passage of the HDZ people through the town?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: To avoid any misunderstanding of this, when I said "unusual," I meant to say that they honked the horns of their vehicles. There were too many flags. At the same time, there were two vehicles driving alongside each other in the same direction along the road. Nobody was against their passage. Had they done it in a peaceful and tolerant atmosphere, things would have been different, but it left a very bad impression, because people began to fear such behaviour. They began to express surprise and to wonder why they were behaving like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say on page 88, line 6, "people began to fear such behaviour," which people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: All those who found such behaviour alien. I assume that all normal people who wanted there to be a normal atmosphere, understanding, confidence, good neighbourly relations, and so on. Of course it was the representatives of other parties who would be most afraid. It's only natural. In this case it would be the SDA, the SDP, and those who were not members of any political party, because there were such people as well, people who hadn't elected to join any of these parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that flags were being shown by the vehicles, or there were plenty of flags, or too many flags, I think you said. Which flags were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: For the most part HDZ flags, but there were also other flags. I think that -- well, it's not that I don't know or wouldn't like to say, but this has to do with what I asked at the beginning of the session. It's enough for now to say that there were others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's move to a further topic. In March, April, 1992, could we say that this is around about the time that the conflict with the Serbs in Bosnia broke out?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I think this is common knowledge. I think that this Court and the public know about this. I don't think there's any need to elaborate on it. Of course, when one bears in mind the barricades in Sarajevo, one might say it was late March, early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Prozor itself, the municipality, directly affected by this conflict?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: No. No. Although in the direction of Kupres, going from Prozor, where it was assumed that lines should be established at the time, but this was a distant and inactive area, one might say that the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The implications of that, why I'm asking this, is simply to get an idea of whether things continued normally in Prozor or whether they were disrupted by the war.

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: In Prozor there was much more disruption than would normally have happened, because probably there were plans afoot which were to be implemented in Prozor, and for this reason it was necessary to create an atmosphere of insecurity, fear, and general confusion in Prozor, not to say an interruption of teaching in schools, for example. There were -- there was intense activity about moving the population out, and so on, or, rather, attempts to move the population out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. What about the Prozor municipal association? Did it continue or was it replaced by another body?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I think one can connect this with the decision on proclaiming an imminent threat of war. When the legislative branch of government ceases to function and the Presidency takes over its role, the extended Presidency, extended with certain members. Bearing in mind that in early April an imminent threat of war was declared, steps were taken right away to suspend the Assembly and establish a war Presidency for Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The imminent threat that was -- imminent threat of war which was declared, by whom was this declared?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: By the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as I know. I think it's correct, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And this is early April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I think it was on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The War Presidency, how long was it created after the 8th of April? This is the Prozor municipality War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Not much time was needed to reach that decision because the War Presidency in Prozor municipality had 11 members, seven of whom were from the HDZ, four from the Party of Democratic Action, and although this ratio does not reflect the proportion according to the population, as the decision was made by the Presidency, it was able to prepare and implement all the decisions it wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This War Presidency, to whom were they directly responsible; the Prozor, or Presidency?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: It was supposed to be responsible to the Presidency or, rather, the higher organs, the legal organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, everything we found out indicated that this responsibility was directed elsewhere and that information was forwarded to another address, not the one to which it was supposed to be forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of which address it is that you're referring to, or any direct knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, and this could be corroborated by a document which, unfortunately, I don't have, but according to the behaviour of the people in the War Presidency, I'm convinced that this was at the centre of the HVO, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as a community that was established, and its name was already starting to be used. Our intuition and my own personal intuition was that, to say the least, basic information was sent there, and it was not sent to where it should have been, and what was sent to Sarajevo was done by others, not at the initiative of the HDZ. There was a problem about setting up a unified staff in Prozor municipality. The representatives of the HDZ did not want to accept it. As Mr. Jerko Doko was the republican defence minister, the information about the problems in setting up the staff was forwarded, and Mr. Jerko Doko expressed his views on the subject. He said that the legal organs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had to be respected, that the flag and coat of arms had to be respected, that a unified Prozor staff had to be established. And this message primarily related to the president of the HDZ, Mr. Ilija Petkovic, who at the time was the fiercest opponent of the implementation both of decisions and symbols of the legal organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may intervene here for a second. The answers are being non-responsive. I don't want to interrupt the gentleman, but if the gentleman could simply answer the question and then I'm sure my colleague here for the Prosecution will lead him in an appropriate manner, but he's going into intuition, speculation. I think if he just sticks to the facts, it will be a lot easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Try and be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We were coming to these matters in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's go through this -- or go back over what you've just told us. The decision of the 8th of April where the imminent war threat was declared, was any instruction issued along with that declaration of an imminent war threat?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: That decision was broadcast publicly, and it was officially forwarded to all the legal organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But did Prozor municipality have to take any action with regard to that declaration?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What action?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: It had to not only establish a war Presidency but also a joint defence staff or, rather, a Territorial Defence Staff, which would be a joint defence staff for Prozor municipality. And the deadline for this was the 15th of April, 1992. Unfortunately, this deadline was not respected, but after lengthy talks at which we learned this - I myself was present there - a compromise decision was reached, and on the 16th of April, 1992, in the early morning, Sarajevo was officially informed about the establishment of a unified defence staff of Prozor municipality. There were enormous problems and lengthy negotiations before this was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was the position of the HDZ with regard to the establishment of this joint defence staff?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: The position of the most extreme part of the HDZ, and probably those who knew of other plans, was that Bosniaks had only the option of accepting the HVO, or, if they did not want to do so, and this was not a voluntary choice, they could join the Chetniks, because they thought that the Territorial Defence was a Chetnik organisation. When I said we had had many problems and lengthy talks, this referred to the search for compromise solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did the HDZ put forward any specific candidates for the joint -- or the defence staff they were proposing?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: After the compromise decision, the possibility was left open. After the 16th of April and over the next few days candidates were to be nominated by both sides, conditionally speaking, to create a unified defence staff for Prozor municipality, as the name was officially agreed on. However, they never actually carried this through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When the compromise decision was reached, were you and the other members of the SDA party happy with the compromise decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the question. Happy? Why is this relevant whether he or somebody else or the party is happy? They reached a compromise. That in and of itself speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with due respect, it's a term of speech. The question is, there was a compromise, but was the witness who was present at the meeting, was he satisfied with that compromise walking out of that meeting? It's simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The answer to that question of yours I can give in part, because a solution was found to avoid a conflict, whereas we were partially dissatisfied because we saw that there was an attack on suspending the legal organs of power and authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in that context nobody could have been satisfied or happy with that kind of solution. But bearing in mind the fact that it was the result of negotiations and talks, which meant that conflicts wouldn't be pursued but that people wanted to live in peace and have the legal organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which were internationally recognised, prevail and what the representatives of the HDZ had asked, and they had asked for something that we didn't know about, which meant the suspension of that first precondition, so I think the question of whether we were satisfied or not is a very good question for all those who were aware of the problems involved during the talks and negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So the result ultimately was that no joint defence staff was set up, but were there any other defence staffs in existence or set up?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes. After a month had expired, the Bosniaks, and of course all the other people who wished to have the option of a Bosnia-Herzegovina republic and sought legal organs pursuant to a request of the republican staff of the Territorial Defence, a staff was set up on the one hand, on the one side, and on the other the staff also was also set up, to the best of my knowledge, and both, later on, had a coordinating role in the period to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: These two staffs that were set up, did they share the same headquarters or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know who headed up the staff of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: During that period we had a number of talks, difficult negotiations, and several times representatives would attend our talks from the HDZ to introduce members of the staff. And when they did so, they would first of all introduce -- they would first of all actually say that -- the first man who came, I think, was Josip Zgela. Whether that was his real name and surname we can't really know, or whether he had another name, but he said that that was an experienced man from Vukovar and that he would help us in the establishment and in finding a solution. The other man had a nickname, or a pseudonym, which was Srna or Do, and they said that he was an experienced warrior as well. And the third man was Andjelic. And the people would change very frequently. We tried to prevail upon the people to tell them that we had a specific situation and that we had very realistic requests that our area should not be engulfed by conflict and do everything in our power to prevent a conflict. Now, some of these people -- I don't know if I'm going to harm any of them by naming them, and that's why I omitted naming names at the beginning, I didn't want to state names, but some people really did show quite a lot of understanding towards the problem at that we all faced, our mutual problem. So it would be difficult to select just a few people. However, these people would change from time to time, but then, of course, we come to the worst period later on and to a commander called Ilija Franjic, who was a local commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that the term "HVO" was starting to appear around about this time. The Croatian leadership that you were dealing with at this stage and the SDA was dealing with, did they describe themselves as HDZ or HVO at this stage?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: They came as representatives of the HDZ, of course, but the HVO -- they used the HVO as the supreme organisation in charge of everything, both for defence and for security, for law and order, for power and authority, and even the HVO for oaths. We had the feeling, not perhaps at the beginning but when they explained to us what the HVO was, we gained the impression that that's -- that there was a military putsch which took care of everything from A to Z when it came to human endeavour, overall human endeavour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In Prozor at this stage, there were therefore two defence staffs, one for the HDZ/HVO, and one for the Bosniaks. Did these two defence staffs cooperate in setting up a joint defence or defence plan for Prozor?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: I'm not a soldier, of course, myself, so I don't know all the details. However, I do know what we talked about at our joint meetings, and I do know that it was a problem. As far as the defence of Prozor is concerned, at that point in time the defence line was over 20-odd kilometres belong towards Kupres, perhaps even longer, in the direction of Kupres. And these are some features where people were sent to, and that's where the Defence lines were set up for the Prozor municipality area in such a way that a sector, I think we can call it a sector or a section of that line was held by one of them, by one set of representatives of the staff, and the other section was held by another set of representatives of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If there was cooperation between the two sides, from your -- what you got to know from meetings that you participated in, were the Bosniaks an equal partner in this enterprise or endeavour?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: If I had to answer in a sentence or in a word, it would be self-love, love of self by the Croatian representatives. There were terrible problems which we tried to overcome. We asked that we send 20 members to the defence line, but they weren't even given a uniform or weapons. But we found a solution to that problem too. So the question you've just asked about the period we're talking about, what I can say there is that there were always problems with flags and the raising of flags up at the line, the defence lines. Logistical problems, supply problems, transport problems, although we had agreed that we had -- we could have a joint logistics. But no, the relationship was not an equal one, unfortunately, and the president of the HDZ at one point said that when we finish with the Chetniks, we'll have to deal with you. So you had to digest sentences of that kind and pass over them. But quite simply it was our firm intention at all cost to retain the peace and to fulfil our obligations to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You referred to the president of the HDZ who said these things. Are you referring to the president of the HDZ in Prozor itself or a different president?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, earlier you had stated that the outbreak of the conflict with the Serbs did not directly affect the events in Prozor -- or did not directly affect Prozor, rather. Could you tell us, the 1991 to 1992 school year in Prozor, did that continue uninterrupted?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: We did not have any repercussions. The front line wasn't close by. There was no shelling. Shells didn't fall on us. It was all a long way away. And at the beginning of April when the decision was taken to interrupt tuition, most of us considered that that was not necessary and that there was no need to interrupt the school year. The children were to go to school in April and May, just two more months, and that it was a great pity for that whole generation not to have completed that school year. They could have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who took the decision to -- to terminate the school year in April?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Those who were in power, who had absolute power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was there any specific body which took this decision?

utterances.speaker: OMER HUJDUR
utterances.text: Well, possibly there are documents about that, but I know that there was no agreement about a decision like that. There was no joint consultation for that decision to be made. And if somebody claims there was, we don't know about it.
